title: Road Trip

jokes.text: Leslie says 'I was thinking about you when I wrote it' about a year-over-year maintenance cost analysis, then immediately tries to cover it up
jokes.setup: Ben thanks Leslie for a mundane government document — a maintenance cost analysis
jokes.punchline: Leslie admits she was 'thinking about him' when she wrote it, a romantic slip in a bureaucratic context, then desperately walks it back
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Leslie's flustered over-earnestness around Ben. The joke works because it's rooted in character — Leslie's inability to conceal her feelings even in the most professional context. The awkward cover ('cause I told you I wanted to read it?') and Ben's charitable acceptance is true to both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was just... thinking about you while writing this report.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because you asked to read it. That's the only reason. You asked me to let you read it, so I was thinking about you reading it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay...

jokes.text: Ben calls Leslie 'Lesliemin' after she awkwardly says 'Benjamin. Ben.'
jokes.setup: Leslie keeps fumbling Ben's name in her nervous excitement, saying 'Benjamin' then correcting to 'Ben'
jokes.punchline: Ben fires back with 'Lesliemin' — a perfectly dry, economical callback to her fumble
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — 'Lesliemin' does enormous work in one word. It shows Ben is charmed and playful, mirrors her fumble back at her, and generates a genuine laugh. The structural symmetry (she fumbled his name, he inverts hers) is elegant. High economy score is fully justified.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What if we came up with a couple nickname? Like... Ben and Leslie could be... Belslie?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No. No, that's terrible. Never mind.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Wow! That was the most sexual tension I have ever seen in a conversation about documents.'
jokes.setup: Ann has just witnessed Leslie and Ben's painfully awkward hallway exchange about a maintenance cost analysis
jokes.punchline: Ann delivers a perfectly calibrated observational summary that names what the audience just witnessed
jokes.explanation: Functions as both joke and expository device. 'In a conversation about documents' is the key comic tag — the specificity elevates it above a generic 'you two have chemistry' line. Ann is the audience surrogate and this lands because the joke was already visible to the viewer.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I just watched Leslie and Ben create sexual tension over zoning ordinances. That's not normal, right?

jokes.text: Leslie: 'We could both get fired.' Ann: 'That's a dumb rule.' Leslie: 'I know!'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains she and Ben can't act on their feelings because they'd both get fired
jokes.punchline: Ann dismisses the rule as dumb; Leslie immediately agrees — undermining her own stated reason for restraint
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient character beat. Leslie's immediate 'I know!' reveals she's been rationalizing, not reasoning. Good character comedy but not exceptionally original — the 'noble restraint undermined by agreement' beat is a familiar sitcom move.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to appear professional and enthusiastic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Right. Professional. Enthusiastic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, here we go. Big smiles, everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm smiling. Is this not enough smile?

jokes.text: Leslie holds up 'Pretty Woman prostitute dress' and Ann says 'I know. I look really good in it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to find an 'anti-seductive' outfit; Ann shows her a dress
jokes.punchline: Ann identifies it as the exact dress Julia Roberts wore as a prostitute in Pretty Woman, then proudly notes she looks great in it
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: first the absurdly specific pop culture ID of the dress, then Ann's complete lack of self-awareness about why that might be problematic. Ann's breezy confidence ('I know. I look really good in it.') is the payoff and fits her character well.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Thanks, Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're... dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Very duo.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The most dynamic duo.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Mm-hmm.

jokes.text: Leslie's unsexy road trip topics: 'The History of the Ladder' article, different dorms at Johns Hopkins, and reading from her Sonicare booklet
jokes.setup: Leslie needs boring, non-romantic conversation topics to suppress attraction during the road trip
jokes.punchline: Her list escalates in mundane specificity: a New Yorker article about ladders, university dorm policies, and reading aloud from a toothbrush manual
jokes.explanation: The joke is deeply Leslie — she's so thorough, so prepared, and so earnest that even her list of boring things is a researched, categorized document. The escalation to 'Sonicare booklet' is perfect absurdist specificity. High character integration because only Leslie would approach anti-seduction this methodically.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I own a prostitute costume and I look really good in it.

jokes.text: Ann suggests: 'Why don't you ask him about his penis?'
jokes.setup: Ann has been earnestly helping brainstorm boring, unsexy topics
jokes.punchline: Her final suggestion is aggressively the opposite of the brief — asking about his genitalia
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection punchline — the audience expects another awkward-but-wholesome suggestion and gets a sharp left turn. Economy is strong (four words does all the work). Not deeply character-specific but effective as a button on the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could get a-fired!

jokes.text: Cut to: 'Pawnee Zoo, monkey speaking.'
jokes.setup: Implied phone call, presumably about Tom's game show plan or a workplace matter
jokes.punchline: A phone is answered with 'Pawnee Zoo, monkey speaking' — complete non-sequitur establishing Pawnee's ambient absurdism
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist background gag that establishes Pawnee's chaotic local government culture. Maximum economy — four words, huge implication. Loses points for character integration (unclear who says it) and structure (it's not really set up, just dropped in).

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need some good conversation topics for the car ride.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: How about asking him about his childhood trauma?

jokes.text: Ron announces he's everyone's boss and the group laughs it off: 'That's a good one, Ron.'
jokes.setup: Tom announces they can do whatever they want because Leslie is gone
jokes.punchline: Ron asserts he IS their boss; the team dismisses this with 'That's a good one, Ron' — treating a true statement as a joke
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke — Ron's authority is so undermined by Leslie's domineering competence that his staff literally cannot believe he's in charge. The irony that he IS technically the boss but is treated like a punchline is perfect Parks & Rec world-building.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Parks Department, this is a monkey at the zoo.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm very busy flinging feces and eating bananas.

jokes.text: Tom's game show origin: 'My favorite movie is Love Don't Cost a Thing, with Nick Cannon, which is based on Can't Buy Me Love, which is based on Kramer vs. Kramer or something, which I think was Shakespeare.'
jokes.setup: Jerry points out Tom's 'Know Ya Boo' is just The Newlywed Game
jokes.punchline: Tom defends creative stealing with a chain of 'based on' attributions that becomes increasingly absurd, ending with confidently misidentifying Shakespeare as the source of a Nick Cannon rom-com
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation from Nick Cannon → Can't Buy Me Love → Kramer vs. Kramer → Shakespeare is perfectly structured absurdist logic, and the closer 'Don't know, don't care' is a devastating button. Deeply Tom-specific — his delusional confidence, pop culture obsession, and complete lack of intellectual rigor are all on display. The joke is quotable, original, and earns its absurdism through character rather than randomness. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm your boss.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ha! Good one, Ron.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Are you going to shove it up your butt? No. I'm gonna test it out on you four bing-bongs...'
jokes.setup: Someone asks what Tom plans to do with his game show idea
jokes.punchline: Tom preemptively rejects a butt-related dismissal before it's even suggested, then calls his colleagues 'bing-bongs'
jokes.explanation: The preemptive 'are you going to shove it up your butt?' is a funny Tom move — he's so used to dismissal he answers objections that haven't been raised. 'Bing-bongs' is a fun Tom-ism. Solid character comedy, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's obviously just The Newlywed Game with a hip-hop name

jokes.text: Tom's list of networks: 'Spike, G4, GSN, Fuse, WOW, Boom, Zip, Kablam, Slurp, Slurp Latin, Slurp HD'
jokes.setup: Someone challenges what network would buy a game show from Tom
jokes.punchline: Tom rattles off real networks before sliding into completely made-up ones with escalating absurdity, culminating in a full Slurp franchise
jokes.explanation: Excellently structured escalation joke. Starts with real networks (Spike, G4, GSN) to ground the audience, then slides into plausible-sounding fakes (WOW, Boom), then pure absurdism (Kablam, Slurp), then builds an entire Slurp universe with regional and HD variants. The structure mimics how real cable TV works (Spanish-language spinoff, HD channel) which makes it both absurd and satirical. 'I love Slurp HD' as a follow-up from someone else is a perfect button. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Everyone steals. You think Shakespeare didn't steal? You think he just came up with Romeo and Juliet out of nowhere? No, he stole that from some guy. And then that guy probably stole it from some other guy. And that other guy probably stole it from a movie.

jokes.text: Someone enthusiastically endorses 'Ultimate Battle Smoothie' as a great show on Slurp HD
jokes.setup: Tom has just invented the fictional Slurp HD network
jokes.punchline: A colleague immediately vouches for a specific show on the fictional network as if it's real
jokes.explanation: The callback works because it treats the absurd premise as established reality, which compounds the absurdism. 'Ultimate Battle Smoothie' is a perfect fake show name. Loses character integration points because it's unclear who says it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We need to program content for NBC, ABC, CBS, Fox, The CW, Univision, Telemundo, HBO, Showtime, Starz, Netflix, Amazon Prime, Hulu, YouTube Red, Snapchat, Instagram, Vine, Twitter, Tumblr, Reddit, 4Chan, Craigslist, the dark web, Slurp, Slurp Plus, Slurp Max, Slurp Ultra, Slurp Platinum, Slurp Diamond, Slurp Infinity, and Slurp Forever.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Yeah, so, basically every dorm allows bed lofting, but the students have really taken to it at Wolman and McCoy.' Beat. 'Did you go to Johns Hopkins?' Ben: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has deployed her pre-planned boring topic about Johns Hopkins dorms to kill romantic tension
jokes.punchline: Ben has somehow picked up the thread and is now earnestly discussing dorm lofting policy at a school he didn't attend, revealed by the deadpan 'No'
jokes.explanation: This callback lands beautifully — the joke is that Leslie's plan worked TOO well, and now Ben has been sucked into the void of dorm lofting discourse about a school he didn't even attend. The 'No' is the perfect deadpan button. It also reveals something sweet about Ben — he's so charmed by Leslie he'll follow her anywhere, even into a conversation about Wolman Hall. Justifies 8+ through structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Johns Hopkins dorms have a really great common area on the third floor, and the RA program is actually top-notch...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, didn't you go to Indiana University?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So you've never actually been to Johns Hopkins.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: The road trip CD: 'Jimmy Carter's Crisis of Confidence speech, Learning to Speak Mandarin, 16 minutes of Old Timey Car Horn, and something called Banjo Boogie Bonanza'
jokes.setup: Ben asks if Leslie wants to play some music; she says she and Ann burned an awesome CD
jokes.punchline: The CD contents are revealed as an escalating list of aggressively unsexy audio: a presidential speech, language learning, car horn sounds, and a banjo compilation
jokes.explanation: The specificity is what elevates this to an 8+. 'Jimmy Carter' (specifically his malaise speech — the most un-fun presidential address), Learning to Speak Mandarin (practical but romance-killing), 16 minutes of Old Timey Car Horn (pure absurdist duration comedy — why 16 minutes?), and 'something called Banjo Boogie Bonanza' (the uncertain attribution is perfect). The escalation works and it's deeply character-specific to Leslie's methodical planning.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I made us a road trip CD. It's gonna be awesome.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Great, what's on it?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, side A is just "Don't Stop Believin'" fourteen times.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because it's the best song ever made. Side B is Nickelback's entire "Silver Side Up" album, followed by a twenty-minute recording of my mother's colonoscopy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Your mom let you record her colonoscopy?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She didn't know. Also, I added some whale sounds, but they're the sad kind of whale sounds.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben discuss the banjo: 'It's an amazing instrument, the banjo.' 'Yeah. I didn't realize it could be this loud.'
jokes.setup: The Banjo Boogie Bonanza CD is apparently blasting in the car
jokes.punchline: Both characters are forced to have a sincere conversation about the banjo's volume — trapped by Leslie's own anti-seduction plan
jokes.explanation: A gentle follow-through on the CD gag. The comedy is in the shared resignation — they're both now earnestly discussing banjo acoustics because of Leslie's plan. Functional and charming but not a standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... quite a sound.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Isn't it amazing?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's certainly... something.

jokes.text: Ron tells a child waiting for a government interview: 'You can wait at that table, and someone will be here sometime.' Child: 'But aren't you here now?' Ron: 'No.'
jokes.setup: A girl needs an interview about government for a school project; Ron is the only one available
jokes.punchline: Ron denies his own existence/presence to avoid government duty — a perfect expression of his libertarian anti-government worldview
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and fully justifies 8+. Ron Swanson denying his own presence to avoid representing the government he works for is both philosophically consistent with his character and completely absurd. The structure is perfect — the child's logical question sets up Ron's illogical but character-true answer. 'No.' is the most Ron Swanson answer possible. Maximum economy (one word punchline). High character integration because this joke only works with Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: You're obviously here to be interviewed.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, I'm not.

jokes.text: Tom's Know Ya Boo intro: performing without the instrumental track, noting 'it's gonna say boo right there'
jokes.setup: Tom introduces his game show
jokes.punchline: He performs the theme intro a cappella and has to narrate where sound effects will eventually go — the DIY desperation undercuts his showman confidence
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Tom's grandiosity constantly outpaces his resources. Narrating where the sound effect WOULD go is a funny detail showing his delusion. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to 'Treat Yo' Self: The Game Show.' I'm your host, Tom Haverford, and this is my co-host, Puppy Dynamite.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Woof woof! Hey Tom, how are you doing today?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm doing great, Puppy Dynamite. Thanks for asking, buddy.

jokes.text: Tom introduces 'Bobby the Boo' — his CGI puppy co-host
jokes.setup: Tom is hosting his self-produced game show pilot in the Parks office
jokes.punchline: He has a CGI puppy co-host — suggesting he's already sunk resources into digital animation for a show that doesn't exist yet
jokes.explanation: The implication that Tom has invested in CGI for a demo that hasn't been pitched yet is an absurd escalation of his entrepreneurial delusion. Works as a character beat.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If you could sleep with any rock star, who would it be?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, me. Definitely me.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Any rock star, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know. Me.

jokes.text: Tom introduces his CGI puppy co-host Bobby the Boo, who clearly doesn't exist — the office workers are just staring at nothing.
jokes.setup: Tom announces he has a co-host — a CGI puppy named Bobby the Boo
jokes.punchline: Bobby the Boo exists only in Tom's imagination/future demo — in the current moment, everyone is just looking at empty space while Tom talks to it enthusiastically
jokes.explanation: Visual gag that works because of Tom's complete commitment. The CGI puppy who doesn't exist is a great extension of Tom's delusional confidence about the show's production value.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My favorite band is The Decemberists.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh cool, I love... uh... all music.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You have no idea who they are.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I totally know them. They're a... band.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've told you about them like five times.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right, yeah. The December... People.

jokes.text: Jerry correctly answers that Donna would pick Prince; Donna is impressed
jokes.setup: Tom asks which rock star each man's partner would sleep with
jokes.punchline: Jerry — the office punchline — delivers an unexpectedly correct and confident answer about Donna's Prince obsession, suggesting genuine intimacy between these two unlikely colleagues
jokes.explanation: The joke subverts the expectation that Jerry would fumble — instead he knows Donna well. It humanizes both characters and is a gentle payoff. Not a big laugh but a warm, well-earned character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God, are you two fighting? This is the best day of my life. I've been waiting for this moment. I even wrote something down.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: "Treat yo' self." No wait, that's not it.

jokes.text: Andy answers 'Me!' to which rock star April would sleep with
jokes.setup: Tom asks which rock star April would want to sleep with
jokes.punchline: Andy, with total confidence, answers himself — because he considers himself a rock star
jokes.explanation: Andy answering 'Me!' is deeply true to his character — his cheerful narcissism about his musical talent. High character integration because this answer is uniquely Andy. The setup/payoff is clean and the confidence of the delivery is funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Government is like a nursing pig. It's bloated, it doesn't work, and it's always got its snout in someone's business.

jokes.text: April's answer is Jeff Mangum from Neutral Milk Hotel — a profound indie obscurity vs. Andy's assumption
jokes.setup: Andy is confident April would pick him; we check April's answer
jokes.punchline: April named Jeff Mangum — the famously reclusive, artistically respected frontman of an obscure indie band — which is completely consistent with April's taste but utterly alien to Andy
jokes.explanation: Exceptionally character-specific joke. Jeff Mangum is the perfect choice for April — an artist known for depressive, surrealist lyrics and extreme reclusiveness. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) it's deeply true to April's personality, (2) Andy has never heard of him despite April mentioning the band 'a thousand times,' (3) Neutral Milk Hotel's music being described as 'sad, depressing, and weird' perfectly captures April's aesthetic. The fight that follows feels real and earned.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I may have made a poor choice of words.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Why wouldn't you pick me?' April: 'I don't know. You're not technically a rock star.'
jokes.setup: Andy is hurt that April picked someone else
jokes.punchline: April's 'not technically a rock star' is both brutally literal and an understatement — he's absolutely not a rock star by any measure — delivered with April's characteristic flat affect
jokes.explanation: April's deadpan literalism is her signature mode. 'Not technically' does a lot of work — it implies she'd consider him in some non-technical capacity, which is both a cut and a compliment. Very April.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: You have food in your mustache.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's insubordination. You're fired.

jokes.text: 'I've told you that, like, a thousand times.' / 'I don't remember.'
jokes.setup: April is hurt Andy doesn't know her favorite band despite her saying so repeatedly
jokes.punchline: Andy's honest, breezy 'I don't remember' — not malicious, just completely oblivious — is somehow worse than a deliberate slight
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is also the emotional truth of the relationship — Andy's lovable obliviousness is genuinely hurtful without him realizing it. The economy is excellent: 'I don't remember' does so much work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, why is 'Marvin Gaye' on our unsexy playlist?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh, that was me. I may have sabotaged Leslie's plan.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Because I want romance, Ben. I want someone to look at me the way you look at Leslie.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Somebody don't know their boo! That's the sound bite that's gonna play when a fight breaks out.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are starting to have a real argument about music and respect
jokes.punchline: Tom gleefully narrates that a real fight is exactly the content he needed, revealing he's treating his friends' marital discord as show material
jokes.explanation: Tom's producer-brain kicking in as his friends fight is a good character beat. The meta quality — him narrating the sound design of the moment while living it — is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This hotel has the most amazing amenities. They have a spa, a fitness center, and a business lounge. It's like they took everything I love about government buildings and put it in a place where you can also get a Swedish massage.

jokes.text: Ron to the child: 'Look, little girl, can we postpone this for another day? It's unsettling having you just sit there.'
jokes.setup: Lauren has been silently waiting at the table as instructed while Ron tries to ignore her
jokes.punchline: Ron admits he's unsettled by her patient presence — he cannot outlast a determined nine-year-old
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Ron — a stoic, intimidating man's man — is defeated by a quiet child. His admission of being 'unsettled' by her sitting there is perfect Ron understatement. Character-specific and warm.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, is this... are you trying to...?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You have an eyelash on your cheek.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, oh my god, oh my god.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to stop. We can't do this. Not here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Bonjour! Je m'appelle Leslie!

jokes.text: Ron's government metaphor: 'It's never too early to learn that the government is a greedy piglet that suckles on a taxpayer's teat until they have sore, chapped nipples.'
jokes.setup: Lauren's report is about 'why government matters'; Ron realizes this is his opportunity to provide civic education
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers a visceral, agricultural metaphor about government greed that is completely inappropriate for a nine-year-old
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes and fully justifies 8.5+. The 'greedy piglet/suckles on a taxpayer's teat/sore, chapped nipples' metaphor is memorably visceral, perfectly Ron (agricultural, visceral, libertarian), and the escalating physical specificity ('sore, chapped nipples') makes it increasingly absurd. Only Ron Swanson would use nursing-animal imagery to explain taxation to a child. Maximum character integration. Genuinely quotable and has become a fan-favorite moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not overreacting. Ben touched my shoulder and I have a very rare condition called Shoulder Blade Hypersensitivity Syndrome, or SBHS. It's when your shoulder blades are too close to your shoulders.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... not a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's very real, Ben. I read about it on a website that also sells colloidal silver and has seventeen pop-up ads.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'I'm gonna need a different metaphor to give this nine-year-old.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered his piglet/nipple government metaphor
jokes.punchline: Ron's only concern is the age-appropriateness of the metaphor itself — not the anti-government content — acknowledging it was perhaps too graphic without questioning his ideology
jokes.explanation: The confessional button on the piglet joke is almost as good as the joke itself. Ron's adjustment is purely logistical — he just needs age-appropriate imagery, not a different message. This perfectly captures his worldview: the anti-government content is not up for debate, only the delivery method. Maximum economy and character integration. The talking head format makes this shine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Our town has a real obesity problem, which means your players will feel right at home here.

jokes.text: Lauren: 'You have mustard in your mustache.' Ron: 'Don't sass me, Burkiss. Let's get started.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just introduced himself formally to Lauren as her government informant
jokes.punchline: A child immediately undermines his gravitas by pointing out mustard in his mustache; Ron responds by calling it sass and using her surname
jokes.explanation: Delightful. Ron's formal authority ('Ron Swanson') is immediately punctured by the mustard observation, and his response — treating it as insubordination and addressing her by surname like a military superior — is perfectly Ron. The child is his equal and he knows it. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, we've worked out a territorial agreement with the raccoons. They get the east side of town, we get the west side. It's actually a very reasonable solution.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's not how raccoons work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, it's how they work now. We have a signed agreement.

jokes.text: Whale sounds on the road trip CD
jokes.setup: After the banjo music, Ben is offered another selection from the anti-seduction CD
jokes.punchline: The next track is whale sounds — somehow even less romantic than a banjo compilation
jokes.explanation: A good continuation of the CD running gag. The escalation from Old Timey Car Horn to Banjo to Whale Sounds tracks a comic logic. Simple but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, I know Pawnee has its problems. But I've come to care about this town. The people here are genuine and hardworking. And there's someone here who believes in making things better, who inspires me every single day to be better. And I'm not just talking about the town anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So before you decide to cut funding or shut this department down, I'm asking you to really consider what you'd be taking away from Pawnee. You'd be taking away the chance for someone like Leslie Knope to make a real difference. And that's something worth fighting for.

jokes.text: Ben discovers an Al Green song hidden in the CD: 'Oh, no, no, no. This is such a great song.' Ann in confessional: 'I want them to get together. Sue me.'
jokes.setup: The anti-seduction CD is supposed to be aggressively unsexy; something changes on the radio
jokes.punchline: Ann snuck an Al Green song into the CD — the most romantic possible song — and admits to the camera she sabotaged her friend's plan
jokes.explanation: The reveal structure is excellent — we see Ben's genuine delight at the song before Ann's confessional explains what happened. The mockumentary format is used well here. Ann as romantic saboteur is consistent with her investment in Leslie's happiness. 'Sue me' is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What's your favorite intimate location?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: My Lexus.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My Lexus.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You both said the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: It's a really nice Lexus.

jokes.text: Ben removes an eyelash from Leslie's face: 'Make a wish.' Immediately: 'Learning to speak Mandarin. Unit three. Get away from me.'
jokes.setup: A romantic eyelash moment — Ben gently removes an eyelash from Leslie's face and says 'Make a wish'
jokes.punchline: The Mandarin CD track kicks in instantly, breaking the romantic spell; Leslie's 'Get away from me' is both directed at Ben and at herself
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured comedy. The eyelash moment is a genuine romantic beat — the audience is momentarily swept up — then 'Learning to Speak Mandarin. Unit Three.' cuts in as a hilarious and cruel reality check. The timing is everything; the CD is acting as Leslie's own romantic interrupter. 'Get away from me' lands because it's ambiguous who she's addressing. Strong structure justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look, I don't need to listen to their music to know I don't like it. That's the thing about great art - it speaks for itself. So if I haven't heard it, that means it's not speaking to me, which means it's probably bad.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I'm allergic to fingers.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just accidentally touched Leslie's face removing her eyelash; both are embarrassed
jokes.punchline: Ben explains his over-reaction by claiming a finger allergy — a completely absurd and medically nonsensical excuse delivered in earnest
jokes.explanation: 'I'm allergic to fingers' is a beautifully economical absurdist line. It's Ben's brand of awkward-nerd comedy — when flustered, he invents a biologically impossible excuse. Maximum economy (four words), highly quotable, and captures Ben's social awkwardness in a single line. A standout micro-joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to take half of your lunch to demonstrate how taxes work.

dialogue.speaker: Lauren
dialogue.line: Wait, why are you taking my food?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Because that's what the government does. Now you understand taxes.

dialogue.speaker: Lauren
dialogue.line: But that's not fair!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Precisely.

jokes.text: Ben's confessional with a photo of his little brother
jokes.setup: Ben is explaining his desire to keep focused; he references 'this' while the camera presumably shows a photo
jokes.punchline: The confessional reveals Ben's 'anchor' is a photo of his little brother — an anticlimactic, sweet visual joke
jokes.explanation: A gentle visual beat. Without seeing the actual photo, the joke is moderate. Works as character texture — Ben has a little brother he's close to. Not a standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, this is so romantic!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what would make it better? More people. Hey! You there, random stranger! Come join us!

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Uh... okay?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Please sit between us. And talk about municipal zoning codes. Non-stop.

jokes.text: Leslie's presentation: '...and our seats have extra cushioning due to the massive size of our average citizen.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making the case for Pawnee to host the Little League tournament
jokes.punchline: She includes the town's obesity problem as a feature — extra-cushioned seats — with total civic pride, unaware of how damning the admission is
jokes.explanation: Great Leslie joke. Her spin on Pawnee's obesity crisis — turning it into a selling point — is exactly how she operates: unfailing boosterism for a deeply flawed city. 'Massive size of our average citizen' is the perfectly clinical phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So it's just going to be us two?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, unless you want to invite someone else. We could invite the photographer. And maybe a few other people. Like a medium-sized dinner party. Forty, fifty people.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying options.

jokes.text: News report: Pawnee's raccoon infestation 'wreaking havoc' at the State Little League Championship — used against them in the presentation
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are making the case for Pawnee to host the tournament; a committee member raises a concern
jokes.punchline: They screen a news report about Pawnee's raccoon infestation at the last tournament — 'Have these little bandits stolen our sense of safety?'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly calibrated Pawnee world-building joke. The news anchor's line ('Have these little bandits stolen our sense of safety?') is a great parody of breathless local news coverage. The raccoon infestation as a documented civic crisis is consistent with Pawnee's absurd problems.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Franklin Delano Roosevelt? Overrated. Massive government expansion, executive overreach, the New Deal was a disaster. He ruined this country.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: But... my teacher said he helped during the Great Depression.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Your teacher is wrong. FDR is the reason we have all these bloated government programs today. Socialism, basically.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to the raccoon concern: 'The raccoon problem is under control. They have their part of the town, and we have ours.'
jokes.setup: The raccoon infestation is raised as a reason not to host the tournament
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defense is essentially that the raccoons have been given territorial rights — confirming the problem is not solved but negotiated
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pawnee lore joke. Leslie's pride in Pawnee makes her defend even the most damning civic failure as a compromise. The idea that the raccoon situation has been resolved via a territorial agreement with the raccoons is absurd but delivered with total conviction. Quotable and rewatch-worthy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're a bright young man. You remind me of myself at your age - before my coworkers ground down my soul and destroyed all my optimism.

jokes.text: Leslie's speech about Pawnee being 'special' — and the camera cuts to her and Ben's faces
jokes.setup: The committee asks what advantage Pawnee has; Leslie begins a sincere speech about the town's people being 'passionate and kind'
jokes.punchline: The speech slowly transitions into Leslie clearly describing Ben — 'really nice blond hair,' 'shocking number of political biographies' — while maintaining the fiction of talking about 'the town'
jokes.explanation: This joke builds slowly and pays off beautifully. Leslie starts with genuine civic pride, and the speech is moving — but then the personal details ('really nice blond hair,' 'shocking number of political biographies') reveal she's been talking about Ben all along. The moment of realization ('Oh God') from both of them is perfect. High character integration because only Leslie could blur the line between civic advocacy and romantic confession this seamlessly.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Here's a little something for you.

dialogue.speaker: Lauren
dialogue.line: Oh, thank you so much, Mr. Swanson!

jokes.text: Tom asks where each couple's 'favorite place to smush' is; April's answer is 'In our bed, I guess'
jokes.setup: Tom asks the romantic/scandalous smush question
jokes.punchline: April's answer is maximally boring and unromantic — 'In our bed, I guess' — the 'I guess' suggesting she hasn't given it much thought
jokes.explanation: April's deadpan, unenthusiastic answer is character-perfect — she refuses to participate in Tom's manufactured excitement. 'I guess' is the funny word. Contrast with Jerry and Donna's genuine enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You rigged the game.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No, I didn't.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yes, you did. I figured it out.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. You got me. That's actually impressive. You know what? You get bonus points for figuring out my manipulation.

jokes.text: Donna's answer: 'Back of my Benz?' and Jerry correctly guesses 'Her Mercedes.' Tom: 'Jerry and Donna on fire.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks where Jerry's boo likes to smush
jokes.punchline: Donna's answer (her luxury car) and Jerry's exact correct guess ('Her Mercedes') — he knows her, he loves her — is a sweet running gag on Jerry and Donna's improbable but genuine relationship
jokes.explanation: Good Jerry/Donna joke. The running gag of Jerry actually having a great personal life (great wife, apparently great sex life in her Mercedes) while being humiliated professionally is a series-long joke. This is a solid instance of it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Pawnee is like... a beautiful woman. Strong, intelligent, full of surprising depth.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: She's got this infectious energy that makes you want to be around her all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And when she smiles, everything just... everything just feels right.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, are you talking about the town or about me?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The town. Pawnee. Obviously the town.

jokes.text: Andy and April's argument about Mouse Rat vs. Neutral Milk Hotel escalates: 'Art is supposed to be happy and fun, and everyone knows that.'
jokes.setup: April defends Neutral Milk Hotel as real art; Andy argues that Mouse Rat is equally valid
jokes.punchline: Andy summarizes his philosophy of art: 'Art is supposed to be happy and fun, and everyone knows that' — a hilariously confident and wrong aesthetic thesis
jokes.explanation: Andy's artistic philosophy delivered with total confidence is both funny and revealing. 'Everyone knows that' — applied to the idea that all art should be happy and fun — is a perfectly Andy claim. It justifies why he plays cheerful rock and dismisses April's taste. High character integration because this is uniquely Andy's worldview. Quotable and rewatch-worthy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm just gonna, uh, use the restroom real quick. I need to go take care of some personal business. Nothing weird, just normal bathroom stuff. I'm gonna go... water the plants. You know, take a trip to the porcelain throne. I'm not doing anything illegal in there, if that's what you're thinking. I'm definitely not doing cocaine. Why would I do cocaine? I have a job. I have a wife. I have a lot of responsibilities. Anyway, I'll be back in a few minutes.

jokes.text: Tom, watching the fight escalate: 'Damn! This game's got juice.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are having a genuine marital fight about artistic respect
jokes.punchline: Tom's response is purely from a producer's perspective — the real conflict is great TV content
jokes.explanation: Good Tom character moment. He's completely amoral about content — genuine pain = good ratings. 'Got juice' is a fun producer-speak term. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann! Code Red! Ben's in trouble!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you use 'Code Red' for everything. Last week you used it because they were out of your favorite yogurt.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That was a real emergency, Ann!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You don't have a code system if every situation is code red. That's just... yelling.

jokes.text: Ron's lunch tax demonstration with Lauren's lunch — taking 40% of her food as 'capital gains tax'
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining how taxes work to Lauren using her lunch as a prop
jokes.punchline: Ron physically takes 40% of her lunch, then comes back for 'capital gains tax' — a visceral, memorable, and physically concrete tax explanation that horrifies the child
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron's libertarian pedagogy reaches its peak here — rather than explaining taxation abstractly, he physically demonstrates it by taking the child's food. The 'capital gains tax' callback is perfect escalation. Lauren's 'But that's not fair.' / Ron's 'You're learning.' is a beautiful button that's both funny and captures Ron's worldview exactly. Fully justifies 8.6.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I need you to be the voice of reason here.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay, Leslie, you should probably not do this thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm doing it.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No, Leslie, trust me, it's a bad idea.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've already started.

jokes.text: Lauren: 'But that's not fair.' Ron: 'You're learning.'
jokes.setup: Ron has taken 40% of Lauren's lunch as a 'government'
jokes.punchline: Lauren's instinctive 'That's not fair' is exactly the libertarian epiphany Ron was engineering; he confirms her conclusion like a proud Socratic teacher
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode and one of the best Ron moments in the series. Two words — 'You're learning.' — do everything. It's perfectly structured as the payoff to the tax demonstration, it's deeply character-specific (Ron as a libertarian Socrates), it has maximum economy, and it's instantly quotable. The joke works because the child's outrage IS the desired lesson. This is the Ron Swanson joke in miniature.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie! I heard the news and I had to come celebrate with you immediately!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chris, now is really not a good time.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Not a good time? This is the BEST time! I am literally experiencing maximum enthusiasm levels right now. My heart rate is optimal, my smile is radiant, and I have prepared a seventeen-point congratulations speech!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chris, the park department just got defunded and we're all being laid off.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's what makes this moment so perfectly poignant!

jokes.text: Chris crashes Leslie and Ben's post-victory moment: 'I had to come up here and celebrate with you. There is literally nothing in this world that you cannot do.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben have just won the bid and are having a tender moment alone
jokes.punchline: Chris materializes with his signature hyperbolic enthusiasm, completely obliterating the romantic moment — and in doing so, prevents the exact thing the characters have been avoiding
jokes.explanation: Chris-as-oblivious-romantic-cockblocker is a great structural joke. His over-the-top positivity and 'literally' habit are in full effect. The irony is that Chris's enthusiasm — well-intentioned as always — inadvertently enforces the workplace rule he set.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Hey guys! So I just used the bathroom and I wanted to let you know that I'm at 94% efficiency. My bowel movements are 23% more regular than the average American male, and my digestive tract is operating at peak performance. I've been tracking it for six months with a spreadsheet!

jokes.text: Ben awkwardly invites the photographer to dinner: 'Hey, we were thinking about going to dinner, photographer. You want in? You wanna grab some grub?... They have great burgers... Come on, photographer. Last chance.'
jokes.setup: Ben wants to have dinner alone with Leslie but they're in a potentially rule-violating situation; he deflects by desperately recruiting the photographer
jokes.punchline: His increasingly desperate attempts to get the photographer to join ('Last chance') as a chaperone reveal his internal conflict — he both wants to be alone with Leslie and knows he shouldn't be
jokes.explanation: The escalating desperation of Ben's photographer recruitment is charming cringe comedy. His claim that 'they have great burgers' before knowing where they're going is a lovely character detail — he's so flustered he's making up facts. The mockumentary format makes this especially funny since the photographer is the camera crew.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, the key to a healthy lifestyle is consistency. I do 200 push-ups every morning, and I track my macros obsessively. Just last week I realized I was consuming 3 grams too much sodium, so I adjusted my entire meal plan.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Chris, we really should get back to work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, I have a meeting in five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, wait — before you go, does anyone want to play Catan? I just got the seafarers expansion!

jokes.text: Ron's button to Lauren: 'And that, Lauren, is how FDR ruined this country.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been giving Lauren his libertarian civic education; we cut back after other scenes
jokes.punchline: Ron has apparently continued his anti-government syllabus to the point of blaming FDR for the country's ruin — to a fourth grader
jokes.explanation: Perfect button line for the Ron-Lauren subplot. By cutting back to 'FDR ruined this country' we understand his lesson plan has been consistent and escalating. The economy is excellent — one line tells us everything about what the off-screen lecture contained.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Burkiss
dialogue.line: You gave explosives to my child!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It seemed appropriate.

jokes.text: Ron gives Lauren a Claymore land mine as a parting gift: 'This is a Claymore land mine. Use that to protect your property.'
jokes.setup: Ron has a warm goodbye with Lauren; he says he has something for her
jokes.punchline: The gift is a Claymore land mine for property protection — Ron's ultimate expression of Second Amendment/property rights values, applied to a nine-year-old
jokes.explanation: A magnificent joke. The setup — Ron's warmth toward Lauren — makes the land mine gift even more absurd because it comes from a place of genuine affection. Ron isn't being malicious; he's sharing his values through the most appropriate gift he can imagine. 'Use that to protect your property' is both philosophically consistent with everything he's taught her and completely insane. Lauren's simple 'Thanks, Ron' adds to the comedy. Fully justifies 8.5+.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You know, April, relationships are all about compromise and communication.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wow, thanks Ann. I'll just tell Jerry that instead of ruining everything, he should try ruining things slightly less. Problem solved.

jokes.text: April tells Tom: 'Your stupid Know Your Boo game made me and Andy get in a big fight. He just sold his guitar, and he's, like, quitting music now.'
jokes.setup: April comes to Tom with consequences of the game
jokes.punchline: The game has caused Andy to quit music entirely — escalating from 'we had an argument' to 'he sold his guitar'
jokes.explanation: A setup for the resolution more than a standalone joke, but the absurd escalation (argument → career change) is classic Andy. Functional comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: 🎵 The pit. The pit. The pit. 🎵

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: 🎵 It's the pit. 🎵

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: 🎵 The pit. The pit. The pit. The pit. The pit. 🎵

jokes.text: Tom's rigged lightning round: makes up questions designed to reconcile Andy and April, including the mac and cheese question
jokes.setup: April asks Tom to fix the damage his game caused; Tom says he can't help
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately runs a 'bonus lightning round' with transparently rigged questions to make Andy feel validated
jokes.explanation: Tom's manipulation through game show mechanics is a good character moment. His 'What do you want me to do about it?' followed immediately by a structured intervention reveals he does care under the showman exterior.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, thank you so much for buying back my guitar. You're the best.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I didn't buy it back. I stole it from the pawn shop. The guy who runs it is a moron anyway.

jokes.text: Andy answers 'Kraft?' for who makes the best mac and cheese in the universe; April said 'Andy'
jokes.setup: Tom asks who makes the best mac and cheese 'in the universe' — a transparently inflated question designed to get April to compliment Andy
jokes.punchline: Andy's answer is 'Kraft?' — a brand — while April said 'Andy.' Andy got it wrong; April's love is revealed
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Andy's humility (he defaults to a brand rather than himself) contrasts with April's answer (him), which is both a character reversal from the band fight AND a sweet reveal. 'Kraft?' is delivered with genuine uncertainty which makes it charming.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I love April so much. Like, we have the best sex life. Last night we—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, no.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: —tried this thing where she wore my police uniform and—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, our intimacy is—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Please stop talking about our sex life to everyone.

jokes.text: April figures out Tom rigged the game: 'You set this whole thing up so I would be un-mad at you.' Tom: 'You figured out April's trying to trick you. That's worth 100 points.'
jokes.setup: April realizes Tom's lightning round is engineered to reconcile her with Andy
jokes.punchline: Tom refuses to break character as game show host — even when caught manipulating the game, he turns April's accusation INTO a game element (worth 100 points)
jokes.explanation: Tom staying in character as host even when caught is a great moment. He pivots from being exposed to incorporating the exposure into the game structure, which is both funny and reveals his creativity. Structurally elegant.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You can drink when you're 18.

dialogue.speaker: Lauren
dialogue.line: But the legal drinking age is 21.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know. The government is wrong.

jokes.text: Ben's confession speech: 'The town has really nice blond hair, too, and has read a shocking number of political biographies for a town, which I like.'
jokes.setup: Ben starts telling Leslie what he likes about Pawnee, then transitions to describing her attributes while still using 'town' as a euphemism
jokes.punchline: The metaphor completely collapses as he attributes blond hair and reading habits to the town of Pawnee
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most romantic comedic moment and one of its best jokes. Ben takes Leslie's metaphor and runs it even further into the ground while knowing exactly what he's doing. 'A shocking number of political biographies for a town' is a perfectly crafted line — specific, absurd, and tender all at once. The structure is excellent because it mirrors Leslie's earlier speech but goes further. Justifies 8.5+ because it's both structurally elegant and emotionally earned.

jokes.text: Leslie's 'going to see a man about some porcelain' bathroom excuse: 'I'm gonna go see a man about some porcelain, you know what I mean? I'm not buying cocaine. I'm going to the bathroom. The whiz palace, as I like to call it. And I'm not calling Ann, so...'
jokes.setup: Ben has just confessed his feelings; Leslie needs a moment to process
jokes.punchline: Leslie's attempt to exit gracefully collapses into a cascade of over-explanations — 'porcelain,' cocaine denial, 'whiz palace,' Ann disclaimer — each more incriminating than the last
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Leslie Knope — when nervous, she over-explains until she's revealed everything she was trying to hide. The escalation from euphe-mism to cocaine denial to 'whiz palace' is perfect. 'And I'm not calling Ann' makes it clear she's absolutely calling Ann. High character integration because only Leslie would make a bathroom exit this elaborate.

jokes.text: Ann responds to Leslie's urgent code: 'Ann, we have a serious code Ben.' Ann: 'Well, it's not really code if you say his name.'
jokes.setup: Leslie calls Ann in a panic about Ben
jokes.punchline: Ann immediately identifies the logical flaw in Leslie's 'code'
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean joke. Ann's logic is impeccable and delivered with perfect economy. Not exceptional but very solid.

jokes.text: Leslie reads her own pre-written script back through Ann: 'Leslie, it's Leslie Knope from the Parks Department speaking to you through Ann Perkins, friend and beautiful nurse.'
jokes.setup: Leslie had pre-written a script for Ann to read in case Leslie got romantic impulses toward Ben
jokes.punchline: The script begins with Leslie introducing herself to herself, acknowledging Ann's beauty, and then proceeding to instruct Leslie not to make out with Ben
jokes.explanation: This is a great Leslie joke because it shows how extensively she planned for her own failure. She wrote herself a formal script, addressed herself formally ('Leslie Knope from the Parks Department'), and even remembered to compliment Ann in the script. The planning is so thorough it's absurd. Only Leslie would prepare this carefully for her own emotional breakdown. The callback to Ann's intro as 'beautiful nurse' is a sweet touch.

jokes.text: Leslie debates herself through Ann: 'No, you... Then, Leslie, Leslie, you don't know what you're talking about.' then proceeds to talk herself INTO making out with Ben anyway
jokes.setup: Ann is reading Leslie's responsible script back to her; Leslie begins arguing with her own pre-written advice
jokes.punchline: Leslie talks herself into overriding her own responsible plan, framing it as knowing better than her past self
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Leslie arguing with her own pre-written wisdom and losing is a great character escalation. Her debate with her past self ('you don't know what you're talking about') is absurdly funny and emotionally true. High character integration.

jokes.text: Ann's 'No. Don't. Stop.' said with zero conviction while clearly rooting for Leslie to go for it
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she's going to make out with Ben despite the consequences
jokes.punchline: Ann delivers the most perfunctory possible discouragement — three monosyllables with no energy — before her 'Yay!' completes the reversal
jokes.explanation: 'No. Don't. Stop.' delivered with zero investment followed by 'Yay!' is a textbook irony joke executed with perfect economy. Ann can't even be bothered to fake discouragement convincingly. The three-word non-objection is highly quotable.

jokes.text: Chris insists on Leslie and Ben staying at his condo: 'Double nonsense. I would love to have you stay with me. Leslie, you can take the guest room, and, Ben, you have to sleep on my couch.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are about to be alone at a hotel; Chris insists they stay with him instead
jokes.punchline: Chris enthusiastically chaperones them by keeping them in his home — his relentless positivity ('Double nonsense') serving as romantic interference
jokes.explanation: 'Double nonsense' is a good Chris-ism — his habit of amplifying affirmations is on display. The structural irony (Chris accidentally enforcing the rule he set) is solid if not exceptional.

jokes.text: Chris on his couch: 'It is literally the comfiest couch you've ever been on.'
jokes.setup: Chris is selling his condo to reluctant Leslie and Ben
jokes.punchline: Chris's superlative confidence in his furniture — 'literally the comfiest couch' — applied to a couch he's making Ben sleep on instead of a hotel bed is an oblivious gift
jokes.explanation: Chris's 'literally' habit and superlative confidence are reliable character comedy. Not exceptional but consistent with his voice.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben's awkward couch moment: 'This is weird.' 'We're on Chris' couch.' 'Yep, we are.' 'And I'm wearing his clothes.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are alone together in Chris's condo after almost kissing; both are aware of the tension
jokes.punchline: Their conversation consists entirely of stating obvious, strange facts about their situation — as if talking about the absurdity of 'wearing Chris's clothes' can paper over the romantic tension
jokes.explanation: The comedy of two people trying to ignore enormous romantic tension by observing mundane facts is perfect cringe/deadpan. 'And I'm wearing his clothes' is a particularly funny specific detail that grounds the absurdity.

jokes.text: Chris interrupts: 'Sorry, I keep myself very well hydrated, and my bladder is the size of a thimble. I urinate roughly 12 times a night.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are alone and building toward something; Chris emerges from the bedroom
jokes.punchline: Chris overshares his medical/fitness details to explain his midnight appearance — his health obsession leading him to casually describe urinating 12 times a night
jokes.explanation: Chris's health-obsession comedy at its best. The logical chain — well-hydrated → thimble bladder → 12 urinations per night — is absurdly specific and perfectly Chris. The escalation to '12 times a night' is the kind of precise absurdity that makes great comedy. His delivery would be completely earnest, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Chris offers to play Boggle at 11pm: 'Well, now I'm up. You wanna Boggle?'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben say goodnight after the tension has been thoroughly doused; Chris reappears
jokes.punchline: Chris treats his third interruption as a fresh opportunity for board games — completely oblivious to what he's been cockblocking
jokes.explanation: 'You wanna Boggle?' is a perfectly economical button for the whole sequence. Chris's earnest offer of board games as the climax of his romantic interference is absurd and deeply character-specific. The word 'Boggle' is funny in this context.

jokes.text: Lauren's mother arrives furious: 'Okay, what exactly did you teach my daughter?... Lauren was supposed to do a paper on why government matters. This is what she wrote. [reads] It doesn't.' Ron: 'Well said.'
jokes.setup: Lauren's mother has discovered what Ron taught her
jokes.punchline: Lauren's entire paper is two words: 'It doesn't.' Ron's response is to compliment the writing
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the entire Ron-Lauren subplot. Lauren has internalized Ron's worldview and expressed it with maximum Swanson economy — two words. Ron's 'Well said' is the ideal response: he's proud of both the content and the brevity. The structure is impeccable — the entire subplot's payoff in one exchange. Justifies 8.7.

jokes.text: Mrs. Burkiss: 'And you ate her lunch? And you gave her a land mine? Really?' Ron: 'Well, it seemed appropriate at the time.'
jokes.setup: Lauren's mother is cataloging Ron's offenses against her daughter
jokes.punchline: Ron's defense of giving a nine-year-old a land mine is 'it seemed appropriate at the time' — completely sincere
jokes.explanation: A strong callback that escalates. The mother's list of grievances (lunch taken, land mine given) recaps the two best Ron gags and forces him to defend them simultaneously. 'It seemed appropriate at the time' is delivered with full Ron sincerity.

jokes.text: April: 'Oh, wow. I didn't realize you were a marriage counselor, Ann.' Then a beat. 'Sorry. My instinct is to be mean to you. I understand.'
jokes.setup: Ann gives genuine, good advice about Andy wanting to feel supported
jokes.punchline: April instinctively responds with sarcasm, catches herself, then explains that meanness is her default setting toward Ann — as if this is a perfectly reasonable disclosure
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character comedy moments. 'My instinct is to be mean to you. I understand.' is extraordinary — April acknowledges her meanness not as an apology but as a neutral fact about herself, as if Ann should simply accept this as a known parameter. The 'I understand' suggests she's sympathetic to Ann's position while doing nothing to change hers. Maximum character integration and deeply quotable. Justifies 8.5.

jokes.text: Ben is excited about 'The History of the Ladder': 'O-M-G. Leslie, I read that same article. It's utterly fascinating.'
jokes.setup: Leslie brings up The New Yorker article on ladder history — one of her planned boring topics
jokes.punchline: Ben has genuinely read the same article and is enthusiastically excited about ladder history — the boring topic has revealed mutual nerdiness
jokes.explanation: A lovely callback payoff. Leslie's 'boring' topic turns out to be a point of genuine connection — their shared enthusiasm for obscure policy/history content is exactly why they work as a couple. Ben saying 'O-M-G' about a ladder article is also perfectly Ben.

jokes.text: Leslie shares cave painting ladder fact: '...the original image of a ladder is in a cave in Valencia, Spain, drawn over 10,000 years ago.' Ben: 'Oh, my God. How about some music?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is enthusiastically sharing the one factoid she knows from the ladder article
jokes.punchline: Ben interrupts with 'How about some music?' — he was briefly excited but has reached his limit on cave-painting ladder content
jokes.explanation: The pivot from shared nerd excitement to 'How about some music?' is a good misdirection. Ben's enthusiasm has limits, and the switch is a funny reminder that even for these two, there's a ceiling on ladder content.

jokes.text: Andy performing 'The Pit' with Mouse Rat — April's favorite Neutral Milk Hotel song reinterpreted as a Mouse Rat song
jokes.setup: April's whole fight was about feeling unsupported in her taste; Andy sold his guitar
jokes.punchline: Andy performs a live version of 'The Pit' — implying he learned April's favorite song and is playing it in her honor, using his stolen-back guitar
jokes.explanation: The resolution of the Andy-April subplot is primarily emotional but has comedic elements: Andy stealing the guitar back ('I actually stole it from his office, but whatever. He's a weirdo.') and the absurdity of Mouse Rat performing a Neutral Milk Hotel song. The callback structure earns high marks.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I actually stole it from his office, but whatever. He's a weirdo.'
jokes.setup: April asks where Andy got back his guitar — he said he sold it
jokes.punchline: Andy casually admits to theft, dismisses any concern with 'He's a weirdo' as if that justifies the crime
jokes.explanation: Andy's ethical framework — theft is fine if the target is weird — is perfectly Andy. The dismissive 'He's a weirdo' as complete moral exoneration is funny and true to character.

jokes.text: Andy's declaration: 'Maybe April doesn't think that we're the greatest band in the world, but, man, she loves me. And I love her. So, you know, who cares. I got the greatest wife in the world! Stop. We're married! We're totally gonna do it later!'
jokes.setup: Andy has resolved his conflict with April; he addresses the crowd at the show
jokes.punchline: Andy's declaration of love escalates into a public announcement about their upcoming sex life
jokes.explanation: Andy's journey from sweet romantic resolution to announcing their upcoming sexual encounter to a crowd is a perfect Andy escalation. 'We're totally gonna do it later!' as a triumphant crowd announcement is both mortifying and completely consistent with Andy's total lack of filter. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Leslie's confessional: 'I think it's good that Chris showed up, 'cause I wasn't thinking clearly.' Beat. Then Ben arrives with receipts.
jokes.setup: Leslie is rationalizing her near-kiss with Ben; the camera catches her saying she's glad nothing happened
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately shows up at her door — after Chris has 'taken off' — putting them alone again and undoing all of Leslie's rationalization
jokes.explanation: The structural irony — Leslie declares she's glad Chris intervened, then immediately ends up alone with Ben — is satisfying situational comedy. 'Uh-oh' is the right button.

jokes.text: Chris's assistant arrives with receipts. 'He's not here. He took off.' Beat: 'Uh-oh.'
jokes.setup: Leslie's talking head just said it's good Chris is there; now the assistant reveals Chris has left them completely alone
jokes.punchline: 'Uh-oh' — the only appropriate response. The camera beat before and after is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic callback structure. Leslie literally just said Chris's presence was good; he's immediately gone. 'Uh-oh' is the right two syllables — it earns economy points for perfect efficiency. The situation has done all the work and the one word is the button.

jokes.text: 'Uh-oh.' — the episode's implicit button as Ben and Leslie are alone again
jokes.setup: Leslie has just said she's glad she didn't act on her feelings; Ben arrives alone with receipts
jokes.punchline: 'Uh-oh' — Leslie's single-syllable acknowledgment that her rationalization has immediately been tested
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — two syllables do everything needed. The episode's final comic beat before the emotional conclusion. 'Uh-oh' is perfectly positioned.

jokes.text: Ron's epilogue advice to Lauren: 'Keep an open mind for a while. Listen to your teachers and read all the books you can. Then when you're 18, you can drink, gamble and become a libertarian.'
jokes.setup: Ron is giving Lauren a balanced parting message after her mother's complaint
jokes.punchline: His version of 'conventional path' ends with 'drink, gamble and become a libertarian' — the trilogy of Ron-approved adult activities
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and fully justifies 8.7. The structure is perfect: Ron appears to be giving conventional parental advice ('keep an open mind, listen to teachers') but the payoff is his version of responsible adulthood: 'drink, gamble and become a libertarian.' The list of three works perfectly — drinking and gambling are vices, but libertarianism as the culminating aspiration is the comic inversion. The sentence structure mimics genuine wisdom dispensing while delivering the opposite. Maximum character integration.

jokes.text: Lauren: 'The drinking age is 21.' Ron: 'I know. Another stupid government rule.'
jokes.setup: Ron tells Lauren she can drink at 18
jokes.punchline: Lauren correctly notes the drinking age is 21; Ron treats this factual correction as further evidence of government overreach
jokes.explanation: The single most elegant joke in the episode in terms of structure. Lauren has genuinely learned something from Ron — she now fact-checks government rules. Ron's response ('I know. Another stupid government rule.') confirms he doesn't view the drinking age as a legal constraint on his advice but as an additional example of government overreach. The consistency of his worldview as a self-contained logical system, even when it proves his own advice wrong, is Ron Swanson comedy at its purest. Maximum economy, maximum character integration. The episode's best-structured single joke.

jokes.text: Mrs. Burkiss asks Ron to write a new paper; Ron asks Lauren to autograph the libertarian one
jokes.setup: Mrs. Burkiss gets Ron to agree Lauren will write a proper report
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately asks Lauren to autograph her 'It doesn't.' paper — treating it as a collector's item, not a failure
jokes.explanation: A wonderful final button to the Ron-Lauren subplot. Ron's request for an autograph treats a child's failing assignment as a libertarian manifesto worth preserving. The joke works because Ron is completely sincere — he genuinely admires the work. Lauren obliging (presumably) is a great final moment.

tmdb_overview: When Chris sends Leslie and Ben on a trip to Indianapolis, Leslie is afraid she won't be able to deny her feelings for him. Ron teaches a young student about his views on government. Meanwhile, Andy gets his feelings hurt by April after playing Tom's new game.
insight: Road trip episode hits 84.9 with 53 jokes—character comedy and deadpan sustain momentum.
